articles.title: Big test for Saint John against Mathews Friday
articles.summary: The goals set at the beginning of the year are all still in reach for the Saint John football team. The Heralds head to Mathews for a Week 8 Northeastern Ath...
articles.body:
The goals set at the beginning of the year are all still in reach for the Saint John football team.

The Heralds head to Mathews for a Week 8 Northeastern Athletic Conference clash.

A NAC championship and spot into the Division VII, Region 25 playoffs for the second consecutive season are all possible for the Heralds.

Coach Bob Dlwgosh, however, realizes Saint John unfortunately controls none of that heading into the matchup of identical 5-2 overall teams.

"We are still just taking a one week, one game at a time approach," Dlwgosh said. "We have to just prepare for the next three weeks and focus on what we can control."

In the NAC race, Grand Valley, at 2-0, currently has the upper hand.

The Mustangs hold a one-game lead in the loss column over both Mathews (2-1) and Saint John (1-1).

St. John, however, lost to the Mustangs 28-14 Sept. 26, and needs help from one of its NAC opponents.

"If it is out of our control, it is what it is," Dlwgosh said.

According to joeeitel.com , which is an unofficial computer ratings site, the Heralds don't even control their destiny in earning a playoff spot despite currently sitting fifth in the current playoff computer standings.

The top 12 teams qualify for the playoffs.

"We are not going to sit around and worry about that," Dlwgosh said.

While Saint John is fifth in the official Ohio High School Athletic Association ratings, Mathews also sits in playoff contention. They are rated ninth in Division VII, Region 25.

All of which is why Friday's game is so important to both schools.

After losing to Pymatuning Valley 31-14 to start conference action, Mathews has won its last three games, averaging nearly 41 points a game in that span.

In addition, Mathews has given up only a single touchdown in its last two wins over Madonna, out of West Virginia, 41-7 and Cardinal 49-0.

"They are a good football team," Dlwgosh said of Mathews. "It's going to be a good matchup."

In particular, Dlwgosh said he is concerned with the mobility of Mathews junior Caden Brubaker.

"Their quarterback [Brubaker] has made some plays with his feet, which is something we need to watch out for," Dlwgosh said. "We had some problems with that against Richmond Heights."

Slowing Brubaker will be difficult, but Mathews has the ability to air it out and stretch the field.

"Having a controlled, good pass rush is important," Dlwgosh said of the discipline his defense needs to have. "They are a fairly balanced team on offense, about 60-40 [run-pass], so we have to be on our toes."

Mathews, too, will have to be ready to defend the Saint John running game.

Tailback Chase Newsome continues to put up big numbers for the Heralds in his senior season. In the 28-22 win against Richmond Heights last Friday, Newsome scored all four touchdowns, rushing for 165 yards on 21 carries.

For the season, Newsome has gained 749 yards with 11 touchdowns.

"I am happy with how Chase is playing right now," Dwlgosh said.

The coach said sophomore Bentley Baker's emergence has helped solidify the ground attack even more.

"We have strengthened our running game and it has allowed us to open up the passing game as the season has gone along," Dlwgosh said.

In the loss to GV, Dlwgosh felt his team didn't finish well as part of the defeat.

Dlwgosh said he has watched growth in his team since then, and hopes to continue the finishing mentality until the end no matter what happens.

"The best we can do is finish out with three conference wins and let the chips fall where they may," Dlwgosh said.

The Heralds head to Northeastern Athletic Confernce opponent Mathews for a Week 8 game at 7 p.m. Friday.

A NAC championship and earning a spot into the Ohio High School Athletic Association Division VII, Region 25 playoffs for the second consecutive season are all possible for Saint John.

Heralds coach Bob Dlwgosh, however, realizes his team unfortunately controls none of that heading into Friday's game.

In terms of control of the NAC race, Grand Valley (2-0) currently has the upper hand. The Mustangs hold a one-game lead in the loss column over both Mathews (2-1) and St. John (1-1).

Mathews still has a crack at GV in Week 9.

St. John, however, lost to the Mustangs 28-14, and and needs help from another NAC school to defeat GV.

According to joeEitel.com , which posts unofficial computer ratings, the Heralds don't even control their destiny in earning a playoff spot.

They are also ranked fifth in the official OHSAA current computer standings.

Meanwhile, Mathews also sits in playoff contention. They are ninth in the Division VII, Region 25 ratings.

After losing to Pymatuning Valley in its league opener, Mathews has won its last three games, averaging nearly 41 points a game in that span.

In addition, Mathews has given up only a single touchdown the last two weeks in wins against Madonna (West Virginia) and Cardinal.

Dlwgosh particularly said he is concerned with the mobility of Mathews junior Caden Brubaker.

Slowing Brubaker will be difficult as Mathews also will air it out and stretch the field.

"Having a controlled, good pass rush is important," Dlwgosh said of the discipline his defense needs to have. "They are a fairly balanced team on offense — about 60-40 [run-pass], so we have to be on our toes."

Tailback Chase Newsome continues to put up big numbers for the Heralds in his senior season. Last week in a 28-22 win against Richmond Heights, Newsome scored all four touchdowns, rushing for 165 yards on 21 carries.

For the season, he has rushed for 749 yards and 11 touchdowns.

The coach said the emergence of sophomore Bentley Baker has helped strengthen the running game even more.

In its lone league loss to GV two weeks ago, Dlwgosh felt his team didn't finish well in part of the the defeat.

Dlwgosh said he has seen growth in his team since then, and hopes that finishing mentality continues until the end no matter what happens.
authors: David Negin, Star Beacon, Ashtabula, Ohio

articles.title: Mustangs earn share of NAC volleyball title
articles.summary: Last week, Abby Crooks and the Grand Valley volleyball team talked about how the Northeastern Athletic Conference title was in its grasp. “We knew we had to...
articles.body:
Last week, Abby Crooks and the Grand Valley volleyball team talked about how the Northeastern Athletic Conference title was in its grasp.

"We knew we had to play our best volleyball, and outwork our remaining in order to win it outright," the second-year coach said.

On Monday night, Cardinal handed the Mustangs their first NAC loss, 25-18, 19-25, 25-22, 25-18.

But Crooks also realized there was another chance to capture at least a share of the conference crown the following night at home against Saint John.

"After our loss to Cardinal on Monday, my message to them [her team] was, 'there's still more volleyball to play,'" she said. "We had to show that our team was resilient and could bounce back after a loss in order to earn at share of the NAC."

Against the Heralds, GV 17-3 (14-1 in the conference) accomplished its mission.

A 25-13, 25-15, 25-27, 25-16 win gave the Mustangs a share of the conference championship with Cardinal. It's the first time GV has won any part of a NAC volleyball title since 2019.

"I'm really proud of our team for learning from our experiences last year, and continuing to push themselves to get better everyday this season," Crooks said. "Winning the conference was a goal from the beginning for us, and we are excited to bring a share of it back to GV."

In the win over Saint John, Rylee Rogers had 13 kills, 14 digs and four aces; Cloe Turk posted 21 assists and Bre Rowland and Rogers added 14 digs each.

But another player made her presence known for the Mustangs, especially the last two matches.

"Something that helped us out both in the Cardinal and Saint John match was Gracyn Ellsworth [who also recorded 14 digs against Saint John]," Crooks said. "Monday night, she came off the bench and gave the girls on the court a spark with great serves and defense. Tuesday night, she stepped up into a new role as libero, and did a great job for us."

Crooks said the defense overall has been strong.

"It's been a big part of our identity all season," she said. "We continue to dig tough balls, stay in system and translate that into offense."

Prior to Monday's loss, the Mustangs captured 15 straight wins. All but three of the matches went 3-0.

Mathews gave GV a battle, before the Mustangs won 3-2 Oct. 1.

GV still has regular-season matches left against Lakeside at home tonight and at Brookfield Monday.

Then, the Mustangs will compete in the Division VI part of the upcoming postseason.

"Our main focus as the season winds down is to stay together as a team and play our best volleyball every time we step onto the court," Crooks said. "We know we have a lot of people supporting and cheering for us, and the girls want to make them proud."
authors: Michael Greco, Star Beacon, Ashtabula, Ohio

articles.title: Primetime Roundtable: The lights are shining bright in Atlanta
articles.summary: The Falcons are putting it all together after two dominant road victories with America watching.
articles.body:
After looking hopeless in the first two weeks of the season, the Falcons have suddenly become one of the league's more prolific scoring teams. Getting Michael Penix Jr. back on the field was necessary for the offense to start functioning at a professional level. Since his return, the team has produced two incredibly impressive road wins, led by a thunderous running game and an ultra-aggressive defense that doesn't commit self-inflicted errors.

Kevin Stefanski, Tommy Rees, and Jeff Ulbrich have worked wonders around certain personnel limitations and injury crises outside the quarterback position. These performances have injected optimism into a fan base that has been looking for any sign of sustainable success. Kevin Knight and Aaron Freeman join me to discuss what has gone into their recent resurgence.

What has been most impressive about what Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees have done to make the Falcons prolific?

Allen Strk: The personnel usage to create more high-percentage looks through the air and varied designs in the running game stands out schematically. It gives Michael Penix Jr. the space to operate in the most comfortable infrastructure imaginable after recovering from his third ACL knee surgery. He is getting the ball out faster and with more conviction into clear passing windows. That improvement led to exceptional efficiency on play-action while still having that explosive element, as shown on his 31-yard touchdown pass to Jahan Dotson.

A heavy dose of 12, 22, and 23 personnel has been effective for the ground game, but Stefanski and Rees are utilizing role players effectively to punish opposing fronts. Kyle Pitts, Chris Blair, and Austin Hooper have been used as fullbacks at various points.

Nick Muse is playing more often to provide more push in heavier sets. Olamide Zaccheaus and Zachariah Branch are being motioned to the side where the run is directed to create space at the second level. These added nuances to the game plan have helped the Falcons produce a jaw-dropping 60.3% run success rate over the last two weeks.

Aaron Freeman: Weaponizing the play-action passing has been the most positive development. The diversity in the run game has also been a welcome addition. Rees and Stefanski are building an offense that marries the run and passing games. It's been extremely effective in Penix Jr.'s first two starts. It'll be fun to watch it grow and develop the rest of the way.

Kevin Knight: The simplest answer is that coaching from top to bottom has improved. The only notable offensive coaches the Falcons had under Raheem Morris and Zac Robinson were Dwayne Ledford and Kevin Koger. Atlanta kept Koger, then upgraded from Ledford to the legendary Bill Callahan.

They also drastically improved their QB coaching with Alex Van Pelt. Tommy Rees also appears to be a significant upgrade over Zac Robinson, who might be one of the worst play-callers in the league based on his early results in Tampa Bay.

In terms of what those coaches have done specifically, I think it's pretty simple: Stefanski and Rees looked at this roster and installed a scheme based on the talent they had available. Such a simple thing, but so very important. It was obvious that Atlanta should've been a run-heavy, play-action focused offense with an explosive passing game for years. In just a month, this scheme looks better than whatever abomination Robinson installed previously.

How does Jeff Ulbrich move forward with Harold Perkins Jr. after his breakout performance?

Allen Strk: Perkins Jr. has seen his playing time rapidly rise over the last two games. Some of it can be attributed to the game script. He played 43 and 52 snaps against Green Bay and New Orleans, compared to only 24 and 26 against Pittsburgh and Carolina. Based on his showing, it could become the norm for the former LSU standout. Perkins Jr. was outstanding last Monday night, showcasing his range, instincts, physicality, and dependability as a tackler.

From cleanly breaking up an out route on Juwan Johnson to running in stride with Alvin Kamara to prevent a big play off a wheel route, the sixth-round pick was up for whatever was thrown at him. Kendal Daniels has played well and provides that downhill ferocity to stop the run.

What Perkins Jr. brings to the table with his skill set makes it hard to leave him off the field, mainly in passing situations. It seems inevitable that Ulbrich will continue to put as much on Perkins Jr.'s plate as possible, given his dynamic capabilities.

Aaron Freeman: With no changes. Perkins is featured exclusively in the team's nickel subpackage, while Daniels gets all the work in the base and big nickel sets. That delineation suits their skill sets. Perkins' superior speed makes him more impactful in space or rushing the quarterback on obvious passing downs. In contrast, Daniels' superior size and instincts make him best suited as a run defender.

The Falcons can keep both players in their current roles without needing to change anything. The only real adjustment depends on matchups. If the Falcons face a bigger, more physical tight end, Daniels is probably the better option. But if it's an athletic player like Johnson, we just saw how effective Perkins can be in those battles.

Kevin Knight: Ulbrich seems pretty committed to a rotation at linebacker, but I think Perkins Jr. will continue to dominate the snap share. He was simply too good to ignore against the Saints, putting out some incredible coverage reps alongside a great all-around performance. After starting the season behind Daniels (67.2%) with a 34.3% snap share, the two have swapped places in the lineup. Over the past two games, Perkins has seen his snap share jump to 65.2% and 70.3%, with Daniels moving into the third linebacker spot.

My long-term view is that the Falcons view both as starting-quality linebackers. The plan could be for Perkins Jr. and Daniels to take over the starting jobs in 2027. To that end, the team would be wise to make sure both are getting live game reps this season.

It's possible that Daniels moves to backup and special teams status if Perkins keeps playing like this, but for now, I'd expect the rotation to continue. I also don't think the team is pulling Divine Deablo off the field anytime soon unless his injuries continue to drag him down. He's a major leader, and his communication is likely critical to how the defense functions.

Have any offensive linemen elevated their play in particular in the back-to-back dominant wins?

Allen Strk: After being a step behind far too often at the start of the season, Jawaan Taylor has picked it up during this road stretch. He plays with a nasty streak the offensive line lacked last year after Kaleb McGary's season-ending injury (and eventual retirement). There were moments in both dominant wins that he mauled whoever was in front of him, whether it was an edge defender or a linebacker at the second level.

Taylor will need to step up against better competition as a pass protector, but his run-blocking gives the Falcons an enormous lift on the right side, with Chris Lindstrom continuing to perform at an All-Pro level.

Aaron Freeman: The Falcons have shown greater down-to-down consistency over the last two weeks by leaning more on the strengths of their various blockers. Lindstrom's athleticism always shines in the team's zone-blocking scheme, but he's also making waves as a puller now that the Falcons are incorporating more gap runs into the mix. But you can't help but acknowledge that the Packers and Saints are far less formidable on the interior of their defensive lines than the Steelers and Panthers are.

That has to be factored into the line's recent success, but they are trending in the right direction. The expectation is that as they get more comfortable with the tweaked run scheme, they should keep being effective as a unit.

Kevin Knight: The biggest pleasant surprise is Taylor, who came in and solidified what had been a very sketchy right tackle spot over the past year. Solidified is actually too conservative a word; he's been legitimately good through four games thus far.

His biggest issues prior to this season were his propensity for false starts and a lack of run-blocking chops. Through four games, Taylor has one false start and has been a boost to Atlanta's #2 rushing attack. If he keeps this up, I think the Falcons will consider giving him an extension.

Ryan Neuzil has also really elevated his game. The scheme change helped him thrive more as a run blocker, while his pass protection has been very solid. At one point, PFN had Neuzil as their top-rated center. He's still ranked very highly. That's quite a jump from last year's largely average campaign. Neuzil is another extension candidate this season.

I should also do a quick shoutout for swing tackle Michael Jerrell, who largely looked like a punching bag in the preseason and at one time looked like a potential cut candidate. Instead, Jerrell solidified the job ahead of the season. When called upon for much of the game against the Saints, he played…solid football.

That's exactly what you need out of your swing tackle. His pass protection is below average, but he might actually be an upgrade as a run blocker over Jake Matthews. I expect Matthews to play in Week 5, but if not, the thought of Jerrell playing is certainly not giving me sleepless nights anymore.

Which defensive player has surprised you the most between C.J. Henderson, Cameron Thomas, and Maason Smith?

Allen Strk: C.J. Henderson's emergence late last season felt more like a feel-good story than the transformation into becoming a capable starter. Facing below-average teams like Arizona and New Orleans gave him a chance to regain his confidence after playing for four teams from 2020 to 2025. Those late-season performances are proving to be a launchpad into becoming a cornerback the coaching staff can fully count on.

Henderson has been tremendous stepping in for A.J. Terrell, starting from opening day when he forced a fourth-down stop being matched up against DK Metcalf. The former top ten pick has already forced and recovered a fumble while producing six pass breakups. That includes three against the Packers, where Jordan Love repeatedly tested him.

Henderson's ability to play tight man coverage and use his length has given the secondary an enormous lift with Terrell on injured reserve. It's been astonishing to see him rise to the occasion for an undermanned defense after nearly falling out of the league.

Aaron Freeman: It's got to be Thomas for me. While Henderson and Smith have both exceeded expectations, both players have flashed before as former high-end draft prospects entering the NFL, so their recent success is less about discovering new capabilities and more about improved consistency.

However, Thomas was expected to be a back-end rotational player brought in to beef up the team's run defense. Instead, he has been a force off the edge as a pass-rusher, outshining even Za'Darius Smith in the last two games. His power and relentless motor have been a pleasant surprise. On a "prove-it" contract, he's well on his way to earning a significant pay raise.

Kevin Knight: Wow, you're making me pick just one? In that case, it has to be Thomas. This man was a rotational run defender throughout his entire rookie contract with the Browns, never playing more than 35% of the snaps and starting just three games. In Atlanta, he was forced onto the field after Jalon Walker's season-ending injury and James Pearce Jr.'s suspension.

I was very skeptical that he'd be anything more than a solid early-down player, but he is well beyond that. Thomas has been one of the NFL's most productive pass rushers (and remains a good run defender) through four games, defying all expectations. He looks leaner, faster, and downright unblockable at times. He signed for $3.1M, making him one of the biggest off-season bargains if this keeps up.

Speaking of which, if he's still playing this way at the halfway point, give Thomas an extension. He's just 26 and could be this team's long-term third EDGE, giving them a dynamic trio behind their two young stars.

articles.title: From 'Lanterns' to Lincoln: Matt Rhule, unbeaten Huskers get their close-up against Hoosiers
articles.summary: Can unbeaten Nebraska finally end its futility against AP Top 25 teams?
articles.body:
Nebraska coach Matt Rhule delivered a one-liner on the button when asked about his cameo in the HBO series "Lanterns."

"I don't know that I'll be taking my talents to Broadway any time soon," Rhule said at his press conference Monday .

Rhule, who has Nebraska at 5-0 heading into a Big Noon Kickoff matchup against No. 7 Indiana on Saturday, has found creative ways to keep the Huskers brand in the limelight the last four years. Rhule's self-deprecation continued when describing the experience, which was filmed in the summer of 2025.

"My daughters were probably more fired up than I was," Rhule said. "They were very concerned I would not get my line right."

Rhule has been handed a familiar script this weekend ahead of the matchup with the Hoosiers. Nebraska is trying to break a 31-game losing streak against AP Top 25 opponents. The twist is it's the Hoosiers – a program that won the national championship in coach Curt Cignetti's second season. In their last matchup, the Huskers had five turnovers in a 56-7 loss on Oct. 19, 2024.

What Nebraska learned from last matchup with Indiana

If anyone told you that would be the state of the program in the 2020s back in the 1990s, or even the 2010s, it would have been laughable. The Hoosiers a national champion? Nebraska losing 31 straight games to ranked teams? Rhule was highly complimentary of the Hoosiers, especially defensive coordinator Bryant Haines – who he met at the Broyles Award ceremony.

"They have a system and they have great players," Rhule said. "They have made a real commitment at Indiana to football. They have the resources to have great players and keep great players."

Rhule's lines were scattered when recalling the memories from that 2024 loss.

"We got in that game – I hate looking back," Rhule said. "I guess I should. I went back and watched it this week. I always look back. I like to feel the pain myself and relive the pain."

Yet there is reason to believe the Huskers can decrease the margins with the Hoosiers this time. Nebraska and Indiana do the same things well. The Huskers are 17th in rushing offfense (231.0 ypg); which isn't that far behind the Hoosiers (252.6 ypg.). Nebraska is second in the FBS in third-down defense (21.3%). Indiana (26.9%) is 14th.

"We're No. 4 in the nation in not turning the ball over since the start of last year," Rhule said before the other half. "But Indiana's first."

Nebraska, however, has a plus-six turnover ratio, which is ahead of Indiana at plus-two.

UNLV transfer quarterback Anthony Colandrea continues to be effective as the replacement for Dylan Raiola, who transferred to Oregon this offseason.

Colandrea averages 278.2 yards of total offense, and in two Big Ten games he totaled 20 carries for 182 yards – an average of 9.1 yards per carry – as a third option with Jamal Rule (333 yards, 5 TDs) and Mekhi Nelson (266 yards, 4 TDs). Huskers fans know that formula well.

"We look at Anthony as part of the run game," Rhule said. "Just like Eric Crouch and Tommie (Frazier)— not to say we're in that league; those are great teams and Scott (Frost) — they were part of the run game here. We're going to make people defend our quarterback. It opens up the passing game.

Colandrea has 1,142 passing yards with 13 TDs and two interceptions – a productive start with offensive coordinator Dana Holgorsen.

"Quarterback-draw with a RPO, zone reads," Rhule said. "We're going to do all of that. They did it with Tim Tebow. They did it with Cam Newton. We have Anthony. We certainly don't want him to get hurt, but we've gotta let him play."

Combine that with a defense that ranks 11th in the FBS with 26 sacks, with six different players have at least two sacks, and perhaps the false alarms of past fast starts are a thing of the past.

Is the play in Lincoln different this time?

Can Nebraska break its losing streak to ranked opponents?

So, here it is. Another huge stage for Nebraska. The Huskers are 0-9 against ranked opponents under Rhule, including a 0-6 record at home. Yet one-score losses to Michigan and USC at Memorial Stadium last season showed the Huskers are getting closer.

The Big Noon Kickoff stage will show the usuals. The sellout streak and a revved up atmosphere from one of the best fan-bases in the Big Ten. That has not changed.

"I think our student section — I think I talk about them all the time. I think they're fantastic." Rhule said. "I understand everyone else is going to make this game about the other team, but a lot of our crowd comes for us."

Rhule has maintained that in four years. He said recruits were texting him after the cameo in "Lanterns." The brand has not diminished under his watch, but a victory in this spot would vault the Huskers into the Big Ten championship and College Football Playoff conversation. There are still matchups on the schedule against No. 13 Oregon (Oct. 17), No. 5 Ohio State (Nov. 21) and No. 20 Iowa (Nov. 28).

A chance to prove it against the Hoosiers comes first.

"We're not a perfect team, so we're going to have to be gritty," Rhule said. "We're not going to run people over, but that grit and that mentality and toughness, hopefully it will show itself Saturday against a really gritty, tough team that doesn't beat themselves."

articles.title: Week 5 Fantasy Football Must-Sit Tight Ends Featuring Hunter Henry & Kenyon Sadiq
articles.summary: Week 5 fantasy football must-sit tight ends include Hunter Henry and Kenyon Sadiq, who face difficult matchups and could disappoint fantasy managers this wee...
articles.body:
We're starting to settle into the season, and not a whole lot has changed when it comes to the tight end picture. Most of the guys you'd expect to play well are putting up points. There are a number of tight ends that have dropped from fringe TE1 down to TE2 or below.

If you're like me, you picked up Sadiq after his breakout performance against the Lions, then put your faith in the Jets to give him plenty of opportunities in Week 4. Instead, New York ran just 32 offensive plays compared to the Bears' 89, and Sadiq goose-egged on four targets.

The Browns also aren't the doormat we thought they'd be when the season started. I expect the Jets to bounce back and, hopefully, spend far more than 20% of the game on offense this week. Still, this is a risk I'd advise you-and myself-not to take with unproven Jets players.

In other words, unless it's Garrett Wilson or Breece Hall, don't be like me and put too much stock into a Jets player based on nothing more than a gut feeling. Because as Jets fans will tell you, the Jets have a way of kicking you right in the gut.

Dalton Schultz took advantage in one of the games that Nico Collins sat out with 12 catches for 140 yards. The rest of the season Schultz has caught just 9 balls for 74 yards, and he still hasn't seen the endzone either. Nico Collins is back in the lineup and will hog up the bulk of Stroud's targets as the two didn't seem to miss a beat after Collins sat out the previous two games. Schultz isn't worth taking a flyer onunless you're completely out of Top 15 options.

Drake Maye finally looked like Drake Maye again, but it still isn't enough for me to put a ton of faith in Hunter Henry going forward. Henry still hasn't found the end zone this season and has only had 15 targets all season and converted that into 12 catches 133 yards. That's just an average of 3 catches and 33 yards per game. Furthermore, Maye did break his slump last week with a big performance against Buffalo, but he's been struggling mightily this season and the Patriots had only scored two offensive touchdowns all season before Week 4. There's still the risk that this is a stagnant offense that got up big for one divisional game, and can regress back to the first three weeks against a Raiders team that looks reborn.

articles.title: Connor Hellebuyck, Dylan Larkin and the NHL Teams and Players Already in Panic Mode
articles.summary: We're just over a week into the new NHL season, and nothing rattles fans and executives like a rough start. Whether it's teams stumbling out of the gate, superstars with an icy touch, or coaches whose seats got warm right away, nerves can get shot quickly.
articles.body:
We're just over a week into the new NHL season, and nothing rattles fans and executives like a rough start. Whether it's teams stumbling out of the gate, superstars with an icy touch, or coaches whose seats got warm right away, nerves can get shot quickly.

While there have been enough teams and players in recent history who overcame tough starts to have great seasons, it's not the most common route to success. An ugly start can lead to sudden changes, and while those changes often lead to better things, for some involved, they can mean the end of the road with their team.

We'll take a spin around the league and look at the teams and players who might already be feeling their stress levels go through the roof, just a few games into the new season.

You have to feel for the Flames. They're saying goodbye to their home, the Calgary Saddledome, after this season and while they'd love to send the old building out with a playoff team and a run to go with it, they've got a very young roster and an overall lack of superstar talent. Rebuilding is hard, and the Flames are already feeling it as the year starts.

Calgary is the last winless team in the league after starting 0-3-0, and what's worse, they haven't even been close in their losses. They've scored just three goals and have allowed 16. They've lost twice to Seattle, 6-1, and dropped a 4-1 decision to Vancouver in between those games. No offense to the Canucks and Kraken, but they're not exactly considered world beaters in the NHL this season just yet.

The Flames have even done drastic things like waiving once-promising forward Connor Zary and then sending him to the AHL when he went unclaimed. For young players like Dustin Wolf, Zayne Parekh, and Simon Nemec, this could be a long, tough year.

We can guess that Connor Hellebuyck misses playing hockey badly, and that he's champing at the bit, waiting for a trade. The Winnipeg Jets going about business and moving on without him, with Stuart Skinner and Clay Stevenson in goal, shows that the waiting won't just be the hardest part; it might take a bit longer, too.

Looking around the NHL at teams that were interested in Hellebuyck before the season started showed a fairly limited market for the three-time Vezina winner and 2025 MVP. Now that games are being played and looking at how those interested teams are playing, you wonder if the market is any different at all and if Hellebuyck's desperation for a change might get him to agree to go somewhere he might not want to play, in a situation that might make playing goalie far more difficult as well.

Yes, we're looking at you, Edmonton. But other teams like San Jose, Carolina, Utah, and Buffalo are all handling things well enough not to make a sudden change. All it takes is one big injury or some seriously poor play at the position; otherwise, Hellebuyck having to wait things out can't feel great for him.

It's difficult to feel bad for Detroit Red Wings former captain Dylan Larkin given his awkward position with the team right now. He asked for a trade and gave management a limited number of teams he'd accept a move to. Now we're a week into the season, and he's not only still a Red Wing but also back on the ice with the team after recovering from an upper-body injury.

The situation isn't what anyone wanted. The Wings would love to have Larkin happy and helping them compete to return to the playoffs, but Larkin would rather be anywhere else than Detroit. Now they have to make it work for each other, no matter how much Larkin gets booed by home fans whenever he touches the puck.

Even though Larkin expanded his list of teams, the wait continues for a trade. He helped his cause by helping lead Detroit to a win over Ottawa upon his return to action, but until this situation is resolved, no one can move on and find closure.

The Panthers came into this season with high expectations thanks to the return to action of a host of players who missed time due to injuries last season. They've started this year 2-0-2, and if that's all you knew about how they're doing, you'd think all was well. But there are big reasons to be concerned.

Aleksander Barkov, who missed all of last season with a brutal knee injury, sustained an injury to his other leg and fortunately will return, albeit not for the next 6-8 weeks. Barkov's elite two-way play and leadership were greatly missed in Florida last season, and any time out of action is a significant loss.

Then there's Brad Marchand, who missed 30 games last season and went down with a lower-body injury in their game against Los Angeles after just returning from offseason surgery. His timetable is yet unknown, but he's remained a highly productive player, and if he misses time, it creates another hole in the lineup.

The Panthers aren't a young team, and they've lost depth over the years from trades and players leaving to get paid elsewhere. Injuries impact teams regardless, but Florida's losses have not been minor and create stress for a team that can be Stanley Cup contenders.

The Kings entered the season with a few big questions to get answered. How they made up for Anže Kopitar's retirement is a big one, but so was how they'd adjust under new coach Peter Laviolette; how Quinton Byfield would adapt to having a bigger role thrust upon him; and how their blue line would fare with Drew Doughty getting another year older and Brandt Clarke looking to take more of the responsibility there.

So far, the stumbles have been more than noticeable. The Kings are 0-2-1 to start the year, and while they've scored nine goals in three games, they've also allowed 15. Thinking back to when Daryl Sutter called the NHL a 3-2 league, and seeing the Kings play in 5-4 games nightly can make you shake your head, mostly because L.A. has always had a strong team defense.

Seeing Clarke, Byfield, and Artemi Panarin being high-event players in their first three games isn't a reason to raise alarms just yet, but it is something to keep an eye on as the games play out. Laviolette likes his teams to be well disciplined defensively as well, and his top guys bleeding goals against can't make him feel good.

The Devils are a team with a load of talent, but they're also a team that, heading into this season, took a calculated risk with their goaltending. A healthy Jack Hughes makes New Jersey dangerous, as do Nico Hischier, Jesper Bratt, Dougie Hamilton, Luke Hughes, and Timo Meier. But with Jake Allen and Nico Daws as their goalie tandem, there was reason to wonder if they'd be able to hold things up.

The Devils are 1-2-0 to start and have scored 6 goals in their first 3 games. They've also allowed 13, and six of those came in a 6-0 blast at the hands of the New York Islanders and a 5-3 loss to Utah, which saw the Mammoth outskating them all game, reason enough to be concerned.

The Devils' talent level is too high to think they could be in serious trouble, but it will bring the offseason choices in goal (trading Jacob Markström to Florida, adding no one else) and head coach Sheldon Keefe's job into the spotlight. New GM Sunny Mehta knows he has a good roster, but having everything click right at the same time in New Jersey has often been a matter of luck.

After returning to the Stanley Cup Playoffs last season and looking renewed under Rick Tocchet's leadership behind the bench, the Flyers were poised to be a hopeful and gritty team moving forward. Despite offseason efforts to make a big splash or two and add more offense to the lineup, they were ready to run it back with a lineup similar to last season's playoff group.

This season hasn't gotten off to the start they were hoping for, though. They're 0-2-2, have five goals in their first four games, and have allowed 17. The goals allowed are bad for Daniel Vladař and Joseph Woll, and they're even worse for Tocchet, who may have suddenly found himself in an increasingly warm seat despite last season's gains.

What's worse is that their offense is averaging just over 19 shots on goal per game, tied with Chicago for the lowest rate at the start of the year (19.3). The temperature is always high in Philly, but it gets ratcheted up even more when expectations are higher.
